D960.about: Schubert’s last piano sonata, composed weeks before his death, a vast, unhurried work of unusual length and serenity, its first movement famous for a distant, rumbling trill in the bass that interrupts the opening melody’s calm and returns throughout the movement like a distant premonition.
D960.ctx: Composed in September 1828, the last of a final trilogy of piano sonatas (D. 958, 959, 960) written in a remarkable creative surge just two months before Schubert’s death from typhoid fever at thirty-one; none of the three were published until a decade later, and all had to wait even longer for wide recognition.
parts: A long, unhurried movement built around a distant, ominous bass trill.
A deeply melancholy, hymn-like slow movement.
facts: The last of three piano sonatas Schubert composed in the final weeks of his life.
Not published until a decade after his death.
Its opening movement is marked by a distant, recurring bass trill.

D958.about: The first of Schubert’s final trio of piano sonatas, darker and more turbulent than its two companions, its opening theme bearing a resemblance to a theme by Beethoven, whose recent death in 1827 weighed heavily on Schubert as he composed this final group of works.
D958.ctx: Composed in September 1828, among the last works Schubert wrote before his death that November, part of a sonata trilogy that shows Schubert directly engaging with the example of Beethoven, whom he had idolized and whose funeral he had helped carry a torch at the year before.
facts: The first of Schubert’s final trilogy of piano sonatas, written weeks before his death.
Its opening theme has been linked to a theme of Beethoven.
Schubert had been a torchbearer at Beethoven’s funeral the previous year.

D894.about: Nicknamed the ’Fantasie’ sonata by its publisher, though it is a true four-movement sonata rather than a fantasy, distinguished by an unusually spacious, unhurried opening movement that Schumann described admiringly as the most perfect in form and conception of all Schubert’s works.
D894.ctx: Composed in 1826 and published the following year, one of the few Schubert piano sonatas to be published in his own lifetime, likely because its lyrical, unhurried character made it more immediately appealing to contemporary taste than some of his more expansive later sonatas.
parts: A spacious, songful opening movement Schumann praised as Schubert’s most perfectly formed.
facts: One of the few Schubert piano sonatas published during his own lifetime.
Schumann praised its opening movement as the most perfectly formed of all Schubert’s works.
Its publisher, not Schubert, gave it the ’Fantasie’ nickname.

D760.about: Nicknamed the ’Wanderer Fantasy’ for its use of a theme from Schubert’s own song ’Der Wanderer’ as the basis for a set of continuous variations spanning all four traditional sonata movements played without pause. One of the most technically demanding works in Schubert’s output, Schubert himself reportedly gave up partway through attempting to play it, exclaiming that the devil himself could play it.
D760.ctx: Composed in 1822, drawing on the melody of Schubert’s own 1816 song setting a poem about a lonely wanderer, the piece profoundly influenced Liszt, who admired its unified, single-movement structure so much that he later arranged it for piano and orchestra and modeled his own B minor Sonata’s continuous form partly on it.
parts: Allegro con fuoco ma non troppo
A bold opening movement built from the ’Wanderer’ theme’s rhythm.
A set of variations on the actual melody of ’Der Wanderer’.
A fugal finale bringing the cycle to a triumphant close.
facts: Based on a theme from Schubert’s own song ’Der Wanderer’.
Schubert reportedly found it too difficult to play himself.
Profoundly influenced Liszt’s own continuous, single-movement forms.

D899/3.about: The most popular of Schubert’s eight impromptus, a serene, flowing piece built on a broad, arpeggiated accompaniment beneath a simple, songlike melody, often compared in mood to a barcarolle for its gentle, rocking motion.
D899/3.ctx: Composed in 1827, the year before Schubert’s death, as the third of the Four Impromptus, D. 899, though the set was not published until decades after his death, and even then with the key of this particular piece altered by the publisher from Schubert’s original G-flat major to the more conventionally notated G major.
facts: The most frequently performed of Schubert’s eight impromptus.
Its publisher altered Schubert’s original key from G-flat to G major.
Not published until decades after Schubert’s death.

D935/2.about: A gently lyrical impromptu built on a warm, flowing melody framing a more agitated central section, the second of the second set of Four Impromptus that some scholars believe Schubert conceived as a disguised four-movement piano sonata.
D935/2.ctx: Composed in 1827, alongside the first set of impromptus, D. 899, this second set was not published until 1839, over a decade after Schubert’s death, and its four pieces’ contrasting keys and characters have led some scholars to suggest Schubert intended them as a unified sonata-like cycle.
facts: Some scholars believe the four impromptus of D. 935 were conceived as a disguised sonata.
Not published until 1839, over a decade after Schubert’s death.
Composed the same year as the first set of impromptus, D. 899.

D780/3.about: Nicknamed ’Air russe’ though the connection to Russian music is likely spurious, the third and by far most famous of Schubert’s six Moments musicaux, a brief, insistently rhythmic piece whose obsessive dotted rhythm gives it an unmistakably folk-dance character.
D780/3.ctx: Composed over several years between 1823 and 1828 and published together as the set of six Moments musicaux, D. 780, this particular piece had actually been published separately several years earlier under a different title before being incorporated into the completed set.
facts: By far the most famous of Schubert’s six Moments musicaux.
Its nickname, ’Air russe’, is likely a later, unfounded addition.
Had been published separately years before the complete set appeared.

D667.about: Nicknamed the ’Trout’ Quintet for its fourth movement, a set of variations on Schubert’s own song ’Die Forelle’ (’The Trout’). Unusually scored, replacing the standard piano quintet’s second violin with a double bass, giving the ensemble an especially warm, resonant bass register.
D667.ctx: Composed in 1819 during a happy summer holiday in the Austrian town of Steyr, commissioned by the amateur cellist and music patron Sylvester Paumgartner, who specifically requested that Schubert include a set of variations on his already-popular song about a trout.
parts: Variations on Schubert’s own song ’Die Forelle’.
D667.sc: Piano, violin, viola, cello, double bass
facts: Its nickname comes from variations on Schubert’s own song about a trout.
Uses a double bass in place of the usual second violin, an unusual scoring for a piano quintet.
Commissioned by an amateur cellist during a holiday in Steyr.

D810.about: Nicknamed ’Death and the Maiden’ for its second movement, a set of variations on Schubert’s own earlier song of the same name, in which Death gently persuades a frightened young woman to come with him. One of the darkest and most emotionally searing works in the string quartet repertoire, composed while Schubert, aware he was seriously ill, was confronting his own mortality.
D810.ctx: Composed in 1824, not long after Schubert had learned he was suffering from what was likely syphilis, a diagnosis that profoundly darkened his outlook; he wrote to a friend around this time that he felt himself ’the most unhappy and wretched creature in the world’.
parts: Variations on Schubert’s song ’Der Tod und das Mädchen’.
facts: Its second movement varies Schubert’s own song ’Der Tod und das Mädchen’.
Composed shortly after Schubert learned of his own serious illness.
Considered one of the darkest works in the string quartet repertoire.

D703.about: Nicknamed ’Quartettsatz’ (’quartet movement’), a single, turbulent completed movement of a string quartet Schubert abandoned after sketching only a fragment of a second; despite its incompleteness, the finished movement is regarded as one of Schubert’s finest chamber works, restless and harmonically adventurous.
D703.ctx: Composed in December 1820, at a transitional point in Schubert’s development as a chamber composer, the fragment was left unpublished and largely unknown until decades after his death, when it was recognized as an important bridge between his earlier, more conventional quartets and his mature late works.
facts: A single completed movement; Schubert abandoned the quartet after sketching a second.
Not published until decades after his death.
Regarded as a key transitional work in Schubert’s development as a chamber composer.

D759.about: Nicknamed the ’Unfinished’ Symphony, consisting of only two completed movements rather than the usual four; Schubert left the manuscript with a friend and it was not performed until decades after his death. Despite, or perhaps because of, its incompleteness, it has become one of the most beloved symphonies ever written.
D759.ctx: Composed in 1822 but abandoned after two movements for reasons that remain unclear — theories range from illness to simple loss of interest — the manuscript sat forgotten for over forty years until the conductor Johann Herbeck rediscovered it and gave its belated premiere in 1865.
parts: A serene, richly melodic slow movement.
facts: Consists of only two completed movements.
Not performed until 1865, decades after Schubert’s death.
One of the most popular symphonies in the repertoire despite its incompleteness.

D944.about: Nicknamed ’The Great’ to distinguish it from Schubert’s earlier, shorter Sixth Symphony (also in C major), an expansive, symphonically ambitious work of unprecedented length for its time, famously championed and premiered after Schubert’s death by Robert Schumann, who discovered the manuscript gathering dust at the home of Schubert’s brother.
D944.ctx: Composed in 1825–26 but never performed in Schubert’s lifetime, the symphony sat unknown until Schumann, visiting Vienna in 1838, found the manuscript and arranged for its belated premiere under Mendelssohn’s direction in Leipzig the following year, praising its ’heavenly length’.
parts: A spacious introduction leading to an expansive main movement.
facts: Discovered by Robert Schumann a decade after Schubert’s death.
Premiered under Mendelssohn’s direction in Leipzig in 1839.
Schumann famously praised its ’heavenly length’.

D328.about: A dramatic setting of Goethe’s ballad about a father riding through the night with his sick child, who is pursued and finally claimed by the supernatural Erlking; Schubert’s setting, composed when he was just eighteen, uses relentless triplet figuration to suggest the galloping horse and distinct vocal characterizations for narrator, father, son and the Erlking himself, all sung by a single performer.
D328.ctx: Composed in 1815 in a single sitting, according to the well-known but possibly embellished account of Schubert’s friends, the song became one of his most celebrated works and helped establish his reputation, even though, like much of his early output, it was initially rejected by the publisher Breitkopf & Härtel.
facts: Composed when Schubert was just eighteen.
A single singer voices four distinct characters: narrator, father, son and the Erlking.
Initially rejected by the publisher Breitkopf & Härtel.

D839.about: Widely known simply as Schubert’s ’Ave Maria’, though it originally set different words entirely — a prayer from Walter Scott’s poem The Lady of the Lake, sung by the character Ellen. The Latin ’Ave Maria’ text now usually heard was fitted to Schubert’s melody only later, by other hands, and does not match his original setting word for word.
D839.ctx: Composed in 1825 as part of a set of seven songs from Scott’s Lady of the Lake, translated into German, this piece — Ellen’s third song, a prayer to the Virgin Mary within the story — became so beloved that it was eventually detached from its original context and is now known almost universally by its opening words, ’Ave Maria’.
facts: Originally set a German translation of a prayer from Walter Scott’s The Lady of the Lake, not the Latin Ave Maria text.
The now-familiar Latin words were fitted to the melody later, by other hands.
One of Schubert’s most widely recognized melodies.

D537.about: A compact, energetic early sonata whose finale Schubert later recycled almost note for note as the finale of his much later A minor Sonata, D. 845, a rare case of the composer returning to reuse an entire early movement.
D537.ctx: Composed in March 1817, during a concentrated burst of sonata-writing in Schubert’s twentieth year, when he was living away from his teaching post and absorbed in composition; the sonata was not published until decades after his death.
facts: Its finale was reused, only lightly revised, as the finale of the later Sonata D. 845.
Composed during a single prolific month in 1817.
Not published until 1852, over twenty years after Schubert’s death.
parts: A songful, gently flowing slow movement.
A driving finale later reused in Sonata D. 845.

D568.about: An expansion and reworking of an earlier, unfinished sonata in D-flat major (D. 567), recast a step higher in the friendlier key of E-flat and extended with a newly added minuet, among the most fully-formed and polished of Schubert’s early sonatas.
D568.ctx: Composed in 1817 as a revision of the D-flat major sonata begun the same year, part of Schubert’s intensive early engagement with the sonata form; it was one of only two Schubert piano sonatas published in his lifetime, appearing posthumously as Op. 122.
facts: A revision and expansion of an earlier, unfinished sonata in D-flat major, D. 567.
Gains a newly composed minuet not present in the earlier version.
One of relatively few Schubert sonatas published with an opus number.

D575.about: A sunny, harmonically adventurous sonata from Schubert’s richest year of early sonata-writing, notable for its wide-ranging modulations within a still fundamentally Classical formal frame.
D575.ctx: Composed in August 1817, one of several sonatas written in close succession that summer as the twenty-year-old Schubert worked intensively to master the form pioneered by Haydn, Mozart and Beethoven.
facts: Composed in a single month, August 1817, alongside several other sonatas.
Noted for unusually free, exploratory modulations for its early date.
Not published until nearly two decades after Schubert’s death.
parts: A bright opening movement with wide-ranging harmony.

D664.about: The best known and best loved of Schubert’s early sonatas, an unusually sunny and lyrical work traditionally associated with the happy summer holiday during which it was likely composed, and with a young woman Schubert reportedly admired there.
D664.ctx: Probably composed in the summer of 1819 during a holiday in the Upper Austrian town of Steyr with the singer Johann Michael Vogl, a period of unusual contentment that also produced the ’Trout’ Quintet, D. 667.
facts: Likely composed during the same happy 1819 holiday in Steyr that produced the ’Trout’ Quintet.
The most frequently performed and recorded of Schubert’s early sonatas.
Not published until 1829, after Schubert’s death.

D784.about: A starker, more turbulent work than its predecessors, composed as Schubert’s health was failing, marking a decisive turn toward the darker, more searching tone of his later sonatas.
D784.ctx: Composed in February 1823, not long after Schubert first fell seriously ill, likely with syphilis, the disease that would shadow the rest of his short life; the sonata’s spare textures and stark contrasts are often read as reflecting this crisis.
facts: Composed shortly after Schubert’s first serious illness.
Marks a stylistic turn toward the sparer, darker manner of his later sonatas.
Not published until 1839, over a decade after Schubert’s death.
parts: A stark, sparsely textured opening movement.

D840.about: A substantial sonata left unfinished, its two completed movements followed only by fragments of a scherzo and finale; its nickname ’Reliquie’ (’Relic’) was given by an early publisher who believed, incorrectly, that it was Schubert’s last piano work.
D840.ctx: Begun in April 1825, around the time of the ’Great’ C major Symphony, but abandoned partway through, one of several large-scale instrumental works Schubert left incomplete during this productive but scattered period.
facts: Left unfinished, with only the first two movements fully completed.
Its nickname ’Reliquie’ reflects an early, mistaken belief that it was Schubert’s final piano work.
Performers today often play only the two finished movements, or complete the rest editorially.
parts: A broad, fully completed opening movement.
A dark, fully completed slow movement.
A minuet left as a fragment.

D845.about: The first of Schubert’s piano sonatas to be published in his lifetime under his own initiative, a large, formally assured work whose finale reworks material from the much earlier Sonata D. 537.
D845.ctx: Composed in the spring of 1825, alongside a run of increasingly ambitious instrumental works, and published later that year as Op. 42 with a dedication to Archduke Rudolph, a rare mark of confidence from Schubert in his own instrumental music.
facts: The first Schubert piano sonata he saw into print himself.
Its finale reuses material from the earlier Sonata D. 537.
Dedicated to Archduke Rudolph, a patron also closely associated with Beethoven.
parts: A broad, dramatically expansive opening movement.
A set of variations forming the slow movement.
An energetic finale reworking material from D. 537.

D850.about: A large, virtuosic and outwardly confident sonata composed during a mountain holiday, sometimes nicknamed the ’Gasteiner’ Sonata for the spa town where it was written, notably more brilliant and pianistically extroverted than most of Schubert’s other sonatas.
D850.ctx: Composed in the summer of 1825 during a restorative holiday trip to Bad Gastein and Gmunden with the singer Johann Michael Vogl, the same journey during which Schubert conceived the ’Great’ C major Symphony.
facts: Composed during the same 1825 holiday that produced the ’Great’ C major Symphony.
Nicknamed the ’Gasteiner’ Sonata after the spa town where it was written.
Notably more virtuosic and pianistically brilliant than most of Schubert’s sonatas.

D959.about: The second of the final trilogy of piano sonatas written in the last weeks of Schubert’s life, celebrated above all for its slow movement, which erupts from hushed simplicity into one of Schubert’s most violent, almost hallucinatory outbursts before subsiding again.
D959.ctx: Composed in September 1828, alongside D. 958 and D. 960, in a final creative surge that came only weeks before Schubert’s death from typhoid fever; like its companions, it went unpublished for a decade and largely unrecognized for far longer.
facts: The second of the three piano sonatas Schubert completed in the final weeks of his life.
Its slow movement contains a famously violent, disorienting central outburst.
Dedicated to Johann Nepomuk Hummel, though Hummel had died before publication.
parts: A hushed slow movement that erupts into a violent central climax.

D899.about: The first and better-known of Schubert’s two sets of Impromptus, four independent character pieces that helped establish the impromptu as a major Romantic genre, ranging from a stark marching theme to a rippling, arpeggiated evocation of flowing water.
D899.ctx: Composed in 1827, the year before Schubert’s death, alongside a wave of other major piano and chamber works; only the first two Impromptus were published in his lifetime, the publisher considering the others too difficult for the amateur market at which the set was aimed.
facts: Only the first two of the four were published during Schubert’s lifetime.
The publisher reportedly judged the remaining two too difficult for its intended amateur audience.
Some scholars have speculated the four pieces were conceived as a disguised four-movement sonata.
parts: A grim, march-like theme subjected to increasingly turbulent variation.
Rippling triplet figuration framing a stormy central episode.
A serene, songlike melody over a gently flowing accompaniment.
Cascading arpeggios surrounding a lyrical minor-key trio.

D899/1.about: A stark march-like theme in the minor, presented plainly and then subjected to a series of increasingly turbulent transformations, closing with a hushed, ambiguous return to its opening idea.
D899/1.ctx: Composed in 1827 as the opening piece of the first set of Impromptus, and, along with its companion No. 2, one of only two in the set Schubert’s publisher was willing to print during his lifetime.
facts: One of only two of the four Op. 90 Impromptus published in Schubert’s lifetime.
Built from a single stark theme subjected to continuous variation.
Its extended length has led some to treat it as a quasi-sonata-form movement.

D899/2.about: A restless, rippling study in triplet figuration that frames a stormy, minor-key central section, prized as much for its technical demands as for its fluent, unbroken momentum.
D899/2.ctx: Composed in 1827 as the second of the first set of Impromptus, published alongside No. 1 while its two companions had to wait decades for print.
facts: Published together with No. 1 during Schubert’s lifetime.
Built almost entirely from continuous triplet figuration.
Its stormy central section shifts to the minor before the opening material returns.

D899/4.about: A brilliant cascade of arpeggios in the minor mode, framing a lyrical, hymn-like central trio, closing the first Impromptu set with its most virtuosic and outwardly showy music.
D899/4.ctx: Composed in 1827 as the last of the first Impromptu set, held back from publication along with No. 3 and not printed until decades after Schubert’s death.
facts: Not published until 1857, nearly thirty years after Schubert’s death.
The most technically demanding of the four Op. 90 Impromptus.
Its outer sections in the minor frame a contrasting lyrical trio in the major.

D935.about: The second set of Schubert Impromptus, four large-scale character pieces of greater weight and formal ambition than their predecessors, the last built as a set of variations on a theme Schubert had used in his incidental music to ’Rosamunde’.
D935.ctx: Composed in December 1827, close to Schubert’s death, and, like the second half of the first set, left unpublished in his lifetime; Robert Schumann later argued the four pieces were conceived as a unified, disguised piano sonata.
facts: Composed in December 1827, less than a year before Schubert’s death.
Not published until 1839, over a decade posthumously.
Robert Schumann argued the set was really a disguised four-movement sonata.
parts: A tender, lyrical piece in gentle triple time.
A theme and variations on a melody from ’Rosamunde’.

D935/1.about: A dramatic, wide-ranging opening piece that moves through several distinct sections and keys, giving it something of the scope and weight of a sonata-form movement.
D935/1.ctx: Composed in December 1827 as the first of Schubert’s second Impromptu set, published only in 1839, over a decade after his death.
facts: The longest and most formally expansive of the four Op. 142 Impromptus.
Moves through several contrasting sections and remote keys.
Not published until 1839, more than a decade after Schubert’s death.

D935/3.about: A theme and five variations built on a melody Schubert had already used as an entr’acte in his incidental music to the play ’Rosamunde’, ranging from delicate filigree to a stormy minor-key variation.
D935/3.ctx: Composed in December 1827, reusing a theme from the 1823 ’Rosamunde’ incidental music, a melody Schubert also returned to in the slow movement of his String Quartet in A minor, D. 804.
facts: Its theme is borrowed from Schubert’s own incidental music to ’Rosamunde’.
The same theme also appears in the slow movement of the String Quartet D. 804.
Consists of a theme followed by five contrasting variations.

D935/4.about: A brilliant, Hungarian-tinged finale full of rapid scales and dramatic contrasts, closing the second Impromptu set with its most overtly virtuosic music.
D935/4.ctx: Composed in December 1827 as the last of the second Impromptu set, its folk-inflected melodic writing reflecting Schubert’s long-standing fondness for the Hungarian idiom heard elsewhere in works such as the Divertissement à la hongroise.
facts: The most technically demanding of the four Op. 142 Impromptus.
Its melodic writing draws on the Hungarian idiom Schubert used elsewhere in his output.
Closes the second Impromptu set with rapid scale passages and dramatic dynamic contrasts.

D780.about: Six short, sharply characterized piano pieces, among the first works to popularize the miniature character-piece as a Romantic genre in its own right, published under a title, ’Moments musicaux’, invented by Schubert’s publisher rather than the composer.
D780.ctx: Composed over several years between 1823 and 1828, with two of the six pieces originally issued separately before Schubert’s publisher, Leidesdorf, gathered all six together and gave the collection its now-famous French title.
facts: Two of the six pieces were originally published separately before being grouped into the set.
The title ’Moments musicaux’ was coined by Schubert’s publisher, not Schubert himself.
Among the earliest widely popular examples of the short Romantic character piece for piano.
parts: A gently rocking piece with a turbulent central episode.
’Air russe’, a folk-like miniature and one of Schubert’s most popular short pieces.
A stark, driving piece in march rhythm.
A wistful, harmonically wandering close to the set.

D780/1.about: A restless opening piece built from an off-beat, syncopated rhythmic idea that keeps the music feeling perpetually in motion, alternating between major and minor without settling.
D780/1.ctx: Composed as the first of the six Moments musicaux, a set assembled by Schubert’s publisher from pieces written across several years between 1823 and 1828.
facts: Built around a persistent syncopated rhythmic motif.
Alternates repeatedly between major and minor within a compact span.
Opens the collection that Schubert’s publisher titled ’Moments musicaux’.

D780/2.about: A gently rocking piece in a lilting compound rhythm, its calm outer sections interrupted by a stormier, more agitated central episode in the minor.
D780/2.ctx: Composed as the second of the six Moments musicaux, one of two pieces from the set that Schubert’s publisher had already issued separately before the full collection appeared in 1828.
facts: One of two pieces from the set published individually before the full collection appeared.
Its calm outer music frames an agitated minor-key episode.
Written in a gently lilting compound meter.

D780/4.about: A flowing, moto perpetuo piece built almost entirely from continuous triplet motion, its restless surface framing a broader, more songful central passage.
D780/4.ctx: Composed as the fourth of the six Moments musicaux, assembled by Schubert’s publisher from pieces composed at different points across roughly five years.
facts: Built almost entirely from continuous, unbroken triplet figuration.
One of the more technically demanding pieces in the set.
Its constant motion briefly gives way to a broader, more lyrical middle section.

D780/5.about: A stark, driving piece in insistent march rhythm, its hard-edged energy setting it apart from the gentler character pieces surrounding it in the set.
D780/5.ctx: Composed as the fifth of the six Moments musicaux, the most rhythmically aggressive piece in a collection otherwise dominated by lyrical and reflective miniatures.
facts: The most rhythmically forceful piece in the Moments musicaux set.
Built on a persistent, march-like dotted rhythm.
Offers the sharpest contrast to the surrounding, more lyrical pieces.

D780/6.about: A wistful, harmonically wandering piece that closes the set, its distant modulations and quiet, unresolved ending giving it a searching, valedictory character.
D780/6.ctx: Composed as the last of the six Moments musicaux, one of two pieces from the set Schubert’s publisher had already printed separately before the full collection was gathered together in 1828.
facts: One of two pieces from the set published individually before the full collection appeared.
Closes the collection with distant, wandering modulations.
Ends quietly and without full harmonic resolution.

D946.about: Three piano pieces from the last months of Schubert’s life, sometimes considered a third, incomplete set of Impromptus, edited and first published forty years after his death by Johannes Brahms.
D946.ctx: Composed in May 1828, just months before Schubert’s death, and left in manuscript until 1868, when Brahms, working through Schubert’s papers, prepared them for publication under the plain title ’Drei Klavierstücke’.
facts: First published in 1868, forty years after Schubert’s death, edited by Johannes Brahms.
Sometimes regarded as an unfinished third set of Impromptus.
Less frequently performed than Schubert’s two published Impromptu sets.
parts: A lyrical, barcarolle-like piece with contrasting stormy episodes.

D946/1.about: An agitated, rondo-form piece built around a turbulent recurring theme, notable for an entire section that Schubert crossed out in his manuscript but which his editor, Brahms, chose to print anyway.
D946/1.ctx: Composed in May 1828 as the first of the Drei Klavierstücke, one of the more editorially contested of Schubert’s late piano works because of the composer’s own deletion of one of its sections.
facts: Schubert crossed out an entire section of the piece in his manuscript.
Brahms, as editor, restored the deleted section for publication.
The longest and most dramatically wide-ranging of the three pieces.

D946/2.about: A lyrical, gently rocking piece with a barcarolle-like flow, its calm outer music twice interrupted by darker, more agitated episodes.
D946/2.ctx: Composed in May 1828 as the second of the Drei Klavierstücke, sharing its key and something of its songful character with the first movement of the roughly contemporary Piano Trio in E-flat, D. 929.
facts: Shares its key, E-flat major, with several other late Schubert works from 1828.
Its calm, songlike outer sections are interrupted twice by darker episodes.
Often singled out as the most immediately appealing of the three pieces.

D946/3.about: A restlessly syncopated finale in bright C major, its breathless main theme contrasted with a more distant, dreamlike central section in the remote key of D-flat major.
D946/3.ctx: Composed in May 1828 as the last of the Drei Klavierstücke, closing the set with music of unusual rhythmic drive for late Schubert.
facts: Built on a syncopated, breathlessly energetic main theme.
Its central section moves to the distant key of D-flat major.
Closes the last piano pieces Schubert completed before his death.

D915.about: A brief, quietly melancholy piano piece written into the album of a friend, its simple ternary form and gently flowing melody giving it the character of a wordless song.
D915.ctx: Composed in April 1827 as an album leaf, a small gift piece of the kind Schubert often wrote for friends and acquaintances, in this case never intended as a public concert work.
facts: Composed as an album leaf, a private gift piece rather than a concert work.
Not published until 1870, over forty years after Schubert’s death.
Its restrained, songlike simplicity has made it a favorite short encore piece.

D593.about: Two independent scherzo movements from Schubert’s early years, lively and Classically proportioned, sometimes performed as a pair though not conceived as parts of a single work.
D593.ctx: Composed in 1817, during the same concentrated period of early sonata- and character-piece writing that produced several of Schubert’s youthful piano sonatas, though the two scherzi were not written as companion pieces to any of them.
facts: Composed during Schubert’s prolific early period of piano writing in 1817.
The two scherzi are independent pieces, not movements of a single work.
Not published until 1868, forty years after Schubert’s death.
parts: A lyrical scherzo with a contrasting trio.

D817.about: A short, folk-inflected piano piece drawing on the Hungarian idiom Schubert absorbed while teaching music at the Esterházy family estate, part of a broader fascination with Hungarian and gypsy-flavored melody that also shaped larger works like the Divertissement à la hongroise.
D817.ctx: Composed in 1824 while Schubert was serving as music tutor to the daughters of Count Johann Karl Esterházy at his summer estate in Zseliz, in present-day Slovakia, where exposure to local folk and Hungarian musical traditions left a lasting mark on his style.
facts: Composed while Schubert was working as a music tutor on the Esterházy estate.
Reflects the Hungarian folk idiom Schubert absorbed during his time there.
One of several works from this period drawing on Hungarian-flavored melody and rhythm.

D365.about: A large collection of short waltzes for solo piano, among the earliest of Schubert’s many published dance sets, reflecting the central place social dancing held in the Vienna of his day and in his own circle of friends.
D365.ctx: Composed across several years in the late 1810s and gathered for publication in 1821, one of Schubert’s first sets of piano dances to appear in print, at a time when he was earning modest income from precisely this kind of accessible, socially useful music.
facts: Gathers waltzes composed over several years before their 1821 publication.
One of Schubert’s earliest published collections of piano dances.
Includes what later became known separately as the ’Trauerwalzer’ (’Mourning Waltz’).

D779.about: A substantial set of short waltzes for solo piano, published under a French title, ’Valses sentimentales’, evoking the intimate, salon character of the pieces within.
D779.ctx: Composed in 1823–24 and published in 1825, part of Schubert’s steady output of dance music for the Viennese salon and ballroom, a genre that provided him with reliable, if modest, publishing income throughout his career.
facts: Published under a French title evoking their intimate, salon character.
One of Schubert’s largest sets of piano waltzes.
Reflects the steady demand for dance music in Schubert’s Vienna.

D969.about: A set of short waltzes from late in Schubert’s life, published as ’Valses nobles’, more polished and harmonically varied than his earlier dance collections.
D969.ctx: Composed in 1826–27 and published in 1827, one of Schubert’s later contributions to the steady stream of piano dance music he produced throughout his career, by this point written with greater sophistication than his earlier sets.
facts: Published under the title ’Valses nobles’ shortly after composition.
Among the last of Schubert’s numerous piano dance collections.
Shows greater harmonic variety than his earlier waltz sets.

D940.about: Widely regarded as the greatest of Schubert’s many works for piano four hands, a dark, tightly argued fantasy in a single continuous span, composed in the last months of his life and dedicated to a young countess he had once tutored and, by some accounts, loved.
D940.ctx: Composed in April–May 1828, months before Schubert’s death, and dedicated to Karoline Esterházy, a former piano student to whom Schubert was reportedly devoted, though the nature of their relationship remains a matter of speculation.
facts: Widely regarded as the finest of Schubert’s many works for piano four hands.
Composed just months before Schubert’s death, in April and May 1828.
Dedicated to Karoline Esterházy, a former student Schubert is thought to have loved.
parts: Tempo I — Fugue: Allegro molto moderato
A return to the opening material culminating in a fugue.

D812.about: A large-scale, symphonically conceived sonata for piano four hands, nicknamed the ’Grand Duo’, whose orchestral scope led some early listeners, including Robert Schumann, to speculate it was really a sketch for a lost symphony.
D812.ctx: Composed in 1824 while Schubert was again working as music tutor to the Esterházy family in Zseliz, a period that also produced several other large four-hand works written for domestic music-making with his students.
facts: Nicknamed the ’Grand Duo’ for its unusually symphonic scale and character.
Robert Schumann speculated it might be a sketch for a lost orchestral symphony.
Composed while Schubert was tutoring the Esterházy family at their country estate.
parts: A broad, symphonically scaled opening movement.

D947.about: A single dramatic movement for piano four hands, given the evocative posthumous title ’Lebensstürme’ (’Storms of Life’) by its publisher, sometimes thought to be a discarded first movement intended for a larger sonata.
D947.ctx: Composed in May 1828, in the same burst of activity that produced the Fantasy in F minor, D. 940, though left as a standalone movement rather than developed into a complete multi-movement work.
facts: Its dramatic title, ’Lebensstürme’, was added by the publisher, not Schubert.
Composed in May 1828, the same month as the Fantasy in F minor, D. 940.
Some scholars believe it was intended as the opening movement of a larger, unrealized sonata.

D951.about: A graceful, songful rondo for piano four hands from the last year of Schubert’s life, lighter in mood than many of his other late works, and one of relatively few pieces from 1828 to see print before his death.
D951.ctx: Composed in June 1828 and published that same year, one of the works Schubert managed to see into print in the months before his death in November.
facts: Published within months of its composition, in the year of Schubert’s death.
Notably lighter and more genial in mood than much of Schubert’s other late music.
One of relatively few 1828 works to appear in print before he died.

D818.about: A colorful suite of pieces for piano four hands drawing on the Hungarian idiom Schubert absorbed while teaching at the Esterházy estate, its final march movement later became one of his most popular pieces in transcription.
D818.ctx: Composed in 1824 during Schubert’s second period as music tutor to the Esterházy family in Zseliz, part of a cluster of Hungarian-flavored works written during and after his time there.
facts: Written for piano four hands, intended for domestic performance with his students.
Reflects the Hungarian folk idiom Schubert absorbed at the Esterházy estate.
Its concluding march became widely popular in later transcriptions.

D733.about: Three marches for piano four hands, the most famous of which, the first, became one of Schubert’s best-known pieces in its own right, widely transcribed and arranged for piano solo, orchestra and other forces.
D733.ctx: Composed across several years and published together in 1826, part of Schubert’s substantial output of accessible, sociable music for piano four hands intended for domestic and salon performance.
facts: The first march became one of Schubert’s most widely recognized melodies.
Extensively arranged and transcribed for piano solo and other ensembles.
Written for piano four hands, a format Schubert used extensively for domestic music-making.
parts: The best known of the three, widely arranged and transcribed.

D898.about: A warm, genial piano trio from the last year of Schubert’s life, more relaxed in character than its companion in E-flat, D. 929, and long a favorite of chamber musicians for its lyrical, unforced flow.
D898.ctx: Composed in 1827, likely close in time to its companion piano trio D. 929, part of a late flowering of chamber music that also included the String Quintet and the final piano sonatas.
facts: Composed in 1827, close in time to its companion Piano Trio, D. 929.
Not published until 1836, eight years after Schubert’s death.
Noted for its warmer, more relaxed character than its E-flat major companion.

D929.about: A large, dramatically ambitious piano trio built around a haunting funeral-march theme in its slow movement, said to be inspired by a Swedish folk song about a fisherman’s farewell; the same theme returns, transformed, in the finale.
D929.ctx: Composed in November 1827 and performed publicly the following March at the only full-length concert of Schubert’s own music given in his lifetime, held less than a year before his death.
facts: Performed at the only public concert devoted entirely to Schubert’s own music in his lifetime.
Its slow-movement theme is said to derive from a Swedish folk song.
That theme reappears, transformed, in the trio’s finale.
parts: An expansive, dramatically charged opening movement.
A haunting march built on a Swedish folk melody.
A large finale that recalls the slow movement’s theme.

D897.about: A single lyrical movement for piano trio, likely composed as an alternative slow movement for one of Schubert’s two full piano trios and later published separately under the title ’Notturno’.
D897.ctx: Composed around 1827, probably as a discarded slow movement intended for the B-flat major Piano Trio, D. 898, later issued on its own by a posthumous publisher who gave it its familiar title.
facts: Believed to be a discarded slow movement originally intended for the Piano Trio D. 898.
Its title ’Notturno’ was supplied by the publisher, not Schubert.
Not published until 1846, nearly twenty years after Schubert’s death.

D821.about: A sonata written for the arpeggione, a short-lived bowed and fretted instrument resembling a large guitar, now almost never heard on its original instrument and instead a cornerstone of the cello repertoire, occasionally also played on viola.
D821.ctx: Composed in November 1824 for the arpeggione shortly after its invention, at the request of a virtuoso of the new instrument; the arpeggione fell out of use within a couple of decades, leaving Schubert’s sonata as effectively its only lasting legacy.
facts: Written for the arpeggione, an instrument invented only shortly before the piece was composed.
The arpeggione itself fell out of use within a few decades, largely forgotten.
Today almost always performed in transcription, most often for cello and piano.
parts: A brief, songful slow movement leading directly into the finale.

D574.about: A lyrical, large-scale sonata for violin and piano, published posthumously as a ’Duo’ rather than a sonata, notable for treating the two instruments as genuinely equal partners rather than piano with violin accompaniment.
D574.ctx: Composed in August 1817, during the same productive summer that produced several of Schubert’s early piano sonatas, and the last of his works explicitly for violin and piano until much later chamber pieces.
facts: Published posthumously under the title ’Duo’ rather than as a sonata.
Treats violin and piano as equal partners rather than a solo instrument with accompaniment.
Composed during the same fertile summer of 1817 that produced several piano sonatas.

D384.about: The first of three short, technically modest sonatas for violin and piano, written as domestic music-making for Schubert’s family and friends, later misleadingly published as ’Sonatinas’ though Schubert himself simply called them sonatas.
D384.ctx: Composed in March 1816, part of a set of three written in quick succession for informal performance within Schubert’s own circle, likely intended for his brother Ferdinand or father, both amateur violinists.
facts: The published title ’Sonatina’ was not Schubert’s own; he called it a sonata.
Likely written for informal performance within Schubert’s own family.
The first of three such works composed in close succession in 1816.

D385.about: The second of Schubert’s three early violin sonatas later published as ’Sonatinas’, a compact, formally assured work despite the composer’s youth.
D385.ctx: Composed in March 1816, written in close succession with its two companion sonatas for domestic performance, at a time when Schubert was still working as a schoolteacher alongside his composing.
facts: Composed in the same month as its two companion sonatas, D. 384 and D. 408.
Published posthumously under the title ’Sonatina’, though Schubert called it a sonata.
Written while Schubert was still working as a schoolteacher.

D408.about: The last and most ambitious of Schubert’s three early violin sonatas, later published as ’Sonatinas’, showing greater formal confidence than its two companions.
D408.ctx: Composed in April 1816, shortly after its two companion sonatas, rounding off a small set written for domestic music-making within Schubert’s circle.
facts: The last-composed and most extended of the three 1816 violin sonatas.
Published posthumously as a ’Sonatina’, a title not used by Schubert himself.
Completed within weeks of its two companion works.

D934.about: A large, virtuosic fantasy for violin and piano built from a continuous chain of contrasting sections, its centerpiece a set of variations on Schubert’s own song ’Sei mir gegrüsst’.
D934.ctx: Composed in December 1827 for the violinist Josef Slavík, one of the leading virtuosos then active in Vienna, and given its first performance the following month, though its unconventional, sectional form reportedly puzzled its earliest audiences.
facts: Written for the virtuoso violinist Josef Slavík.
Its central variations are built on Schubert’s own song ’Sei mir gegrüsst’.
Its unusual, continuous form reportedly confused audiences at its 1828 premiere.

D802.about: A theme and variations for flute and piano built on Schubert’s own song ’Trockne Blumen’ from the cycle ’Die schöne Müllerin’, written for and premiered by a leading Viennese flute virtuoso of the day.
D802.ctx: Composed in January 1824 for the flutist Ferdinand Bogner, drawing its theme from a song Schubert had completed only months earlier as part of ’Die schöne Müllerin’.
facts: Written for the Viennese flute virtuoso Ferdinand Bogner.
Its theme is drawn from the song ’Trockne Blumen’ in ’Die schöne Müllerin’.
Composed within months of finishing the song cycle it draws on.

D956.about: Widely considered among the greatest works in the chamber repertoire, composed in the last two months of Schubert’s life and unusually scored for two cellos rather than the more customary two violas, giving it an especially dark, rich sonority.
D956.ctx: Composed in September 1828, two months before Schubert’s death, and never performed or published in his lifetime; it waited over two decades for its premiere and a quarter-century for publication.
facts: Composed in the final two months of Schubert’s life.
Unusually scored for two cellos instead of the more common two violas.
Not performed publicly until 1850, over twenty years after it was written.
parts: A profoundly still slow movement with a turbulent central episode.
A vigorous scherzo with a somber trio.
A dance-like finale with Hungarian-tinged rhythms.

D804.about: Nicknamed ’Rosamunde’ for a slow movement that reuses an entr’acte from Schubert’s incidental music to the play of that name, the only string quartet Schubert saw published in his lifetime.
D804.ctx: Composed in early 1824, not long after Schubert had learned of his own serious illness, and premiered that March by the Schuppanzigh Quartet, the ensemble closely associated with Beethoven’s late quartets.
facts: The only Schubert string quartet published during his lifetime.
Its slow movement reuses music from the incidental music to ’Rosamunde’.
Premiered by the Schuppanzigh Quartet, best known for its association with Beethoven.
parts: A slow movement drawn from the ’Rosamunde’ incidental music.
A wistful minuet quoting one of Schubert’s own songs.

D887.about: The last and longest of Schubert’s string quartets, a dark, harmonically restless work whose opening bars, alternating abruptly between major and minor, set the tone for one of his most emotionally turbulent chamber works.
D887.ctx: Composed in June 1826, given a single private play-through that year but never performed publicly or published in Schubert’s lifetime, part of a run of increasingly ambitious chamber works from his final years.
facts: The longest of Schubert’s string quartets.
Received only a single private reading during Schubert’s lifetime.
Not published until 1851, over two decades after his death.
parts: An opening movement built on abrupt major–minor contrasts.

D803.about: A large-scale octet modeled closely on Beethoven’s Septet, commissioned by a wealthy amateur clarinetist who specifically requested a companion piece to that earlier work, expanded with an additional violin.
D803.ctx: Composed in early 1824 on commission from Count Ferdinand Troyer, an amateur clarinetist in the household of Archduke Rudolph, who asked Schubert for a work modeled on Beethoven’s popular Septet, Op. 20.
facts: Commissioned as a deliberate companion piece to Beethoven’s Septet, Op. 20.
Its commissioner, Count Troyer, was an amateur clarinetist who played in its premiere.
Expands Beethoven’s septet scoring by the addition of a second violin.
parts: A slow introduction leading to an expansive opening movement.
A dramatic slow introduction leading to a spirited finale.
D803.sc: Clarinet, bassoon, horn, 2 violins, viola, cello, double bass

D82.about: Schubert’s first completed symphony, written while he was still a teenage student, a confident and skillfully orchestrated work modeled closely on the Classical symphonic style of Haydn and early Beethoven.
D82.ctx: Composed between October 1813 and Schubert’s sixteenth birthday that month, while he was a student at the imperial choir school, and likely performed by the school’s student orchestra, in which Schubert himself played violin.
facts: Schubert’s first completed symphony, written at age sixteen.
Composed while Schubert was a student at Vienna’s imperial choir school.
Likely first performed by the school’s own student orchestra.
parts: A slow introduction leading to a spirited main movement.

D125.about: Schubert’s second symphony, a lively and increasingly assured work that already shows a marked advance in orchestral handling over his First, composed while he was still a teenager working as a schoolteacher.
D125.ctx: Composed between December 1814 and March 1815, while Schubert was working as an assistant in his father’s school, a demanding job he found increasingly at odds with his growing ambitions as a composer.
facts: Composed while Schubert was working as an assistant schoolteacher.
Shows marked growth in orchestral confidence over his First Symphony.
Not published until 1885, well over half a century after Schubert’s death.
parts: A slow introduction leading to an energetic main movement.

D200.about: A compact, high-spirited symphony composed with astonishing speed even by Schubert’s prolific standards, reportedly completed within a matter of days during one of his most productive years.
D200.ctx: Composed in July 1815, during a year in which the eighteen-year-old Schubert, still teaching at his father’s school, produced an extraordinary volume of music including well over a hundred songs.
facts: Composed with remarkable speed even by Schubert’s standards.
Written during 1815, one of the most productive single years of his career.
Not published until 1881, more than fifty years after Schubert’s death.
parts: A stately introduction leading to a lively main movement.

D417.about: Nicknamed the ’Tragic’ by Schubert himself, his fourth symphony and the first to move decisively toward a darker, more dramatic idiom, opening with a slow introduction of unusual intensity for a composer not yet twenty.
D417.ctx: Composed in April 1816, the only one of Schubert’s early symphonies to carry a title of his own devising, reflecting a brief but marked turn toward Beethovenian drama and minor-key intensity.
facts: The only early Schubert symphony to carry a nickname supplied by the composer himself.
Opens with an unusually dark and dramatic slow introduction.
Composed when Schubert was just nineteen.
parts: A dark, dramatic introduction leading to a turbulent main movement.

D485.about: A graceful, Mozartean symphony scored for a smaller-than-usual orchestra without clarinets, trumpets or timpani, often considered the most immediately charming of Schubert’s early symphonies.
D485.ctx: Composed in September–October 1816, shortly after the darker Fourth Symphony, marking a deliberate return to a lighter, more intimate Classical idiom modeled closely on Mozart.
facts: Scored for a reduced orchestra, omitting clarinets, trumpets and timpani.
Composed immediately after the darker ’Tragic’ Symphony.
Widely regarded as the most Mozartean of Schubert’s symphonies.

D589.about: Nicknamed the ’Little C major’ to distinguish it from the much larger ’Great’ Ninth Symphony in the same key, a genial, Rossini-influenced work reflecting the craze for Italian opera then sweeping Vienna.
D589.ctx: Composed between 1817 and 1818, at a time when Gioachino Rossini’s operas were the sensation of Viennese musical life, an influence audibly reflected in the symphony’s melodic style and orchestral color.
facts: Nicknamed the ’Little C major’ to distinguish it from the later ’Great’ Symphony in the same key.
Shows the marked influence of Rossini, whose operas were then dominating Vienna.
One of the few early Schubert symphonies published in his lifetime.
parts: A slow introduction leading to a genial main movement.

D797.about: Incidental music written for a now largely forgotten play, ’Rosamunde, Princess of Cyprus’, which closed after only two performances; the music, by contrast, quickly became and has remained one of Schubert’s most beloved orchestral scores.
D797.ctx: Composed at speed in late 1823 for a play by Helmina von Chézy that premiered in Vienna in December that year and flopped almost immediately, leaving Schubert’s incidental music to outlive by far the drama it was written to accompany.
facts: Written for a play that closed after only two performances.
The music has far outlived the now-forgotten drama it accompanied.
Its themes were reused by Schubert in later works, including the String Quartet D. 804 and Impromptu D. 935 No. 3.
parts: An overture, often performed under the title of the earlier opera ’Die Zauberharfe’.
A melody later reused in the String Quartet D. 804.

D795.about: The first of Schubert’s two great song cycles, twenty songs tracing a miller’s apprentice who falls in love, is spurned, and drowns himself in the brook that has narrated his story throughout, setting poems by Wilhelm Müller.
D795.ctx: Composed in 1823 while Schubert was seriously ill for the first time, drawing on a cycle of poems by Wilhelm Müller that had already been set, in an amateur theatrical version, by members of Schubert’s own social circle before he made it his own.
facts: Sets twenty poems by Wilhelm Müller tracing a single narrative arc.
Composed in 1823, during Schubert’s first serious illness.
One of the two works, alongside ’Winterreise’, credited with establishing the song cycle as a major Romantic genre.

D911.about: Schubert’s second and darker song cycle, twenty-four songs following a rejected lover’s solitary winter wandering toward despair and isolation, widely regarded as one of the supreme achievements of the art song.
D911.ctx: Composed in two parts during 1827, the year before Schubert’s death, on poems by Wilhelm Müller; Schubert reportedly told friends the songs affected him more deeply than anything he had written, and their bleakness unsettled some early listeners.
facts: Sets twenty-four poems by Wilhelm Müller, composed in two separate batches during 1827.
Schubert reportedly said these songs moved him more than any others he had written.
Widely regarded as one of the greatest achievements in the entire song repertoire.

D911/5.about: The fifth song of ’Winterreise’, in which the wanderer pauses beside a linden tree that once offered him comfort, its gentle, folk-like melody masking the deepening despair of the cycle around it.
D911/5.ctx: Composed in 1827 as part of the first half of ’Winterreise’, one of the most instantly recognizable songs in the cycle and, in later arrangements, one of the most widely known melodies Schubert ever wrote.
facts: One of the best-known individual songs from ’Winterreise’.
Its melody became widely familiar through later choral and instrumental arrangements.
Its deceptively gentle, folk-like tone masks the surrounding cycle’s deepening despair.

D957.about: A collection of fourteen songs from the very last months of Schubert’s life, gathered and given its evocative title, ’Swan Song’, by a publisher after his death rather than conceived by Schubert as a unified cycle.
D957.ctx: Composed in August–October 1828, weeks before Schubert’s death in November, setting poems by three different poets, Rellstab, Heine and Seidl; the publisher’s decision to present them together as a single collection created the enduring impression of a final artistic statement.
facts: Assembled and titled by Schubert’s publisher after his death, not conceived as a cycle by Schubert himself.
Sets poems by three different poets: Rellstab, Heine and Seidl.
Composed in the final months before Schubert’s death in November 1828.

D957/4.about: A serenade sung by a lover outside his beloved’s window, its gently rocking guitar-like accompaniment and yearning melody making it one of Schubert’s single most famous songs.
D957/4.ctx: Composed in 1828 as part of the collection posthumously published as ’Schwanengesang’, setting a poem by Ludwig Rellstab, and among the most widely performed and arranged of all Schubert songs.
facts: One of the most frequently performed and arranged of all Schubert’s songs.
Its accompaniment imitates the strumming of a guitar.
Sets a poem by Ludwig Rellstab.

D118.about: Often called the first true German art song, a setting of a scene from Goethe’s ’Faust’ in which Gretchen, spinning at her wheel, is consumed by longing for Faust; its restless accompaniment famously mimics the turning of the spinning wheel, which falters and stops as her thoughts overwhelm her.
D118.ctx: Composed in October 1814, when Schubert was just seventeen, a work later credited by scholars with essentially inventing the modern art song by fusing poetry, vocal line and piano accompaniment into a single dramatic conception.
facts: Composed when Schubert was seventeen and often cited as the birth of the modern art song.
Its piano figuration imitates a spinning wheel, which halts as the singer’s emotion overwhelms her.
Sets a scene from Goethe’s ’Faust’.

D257.about: A deceptively simple, folk-like setting of Goethe’s poem about a boy and a wild rose, its strophic melody so immediately memorable that it has since entered the German folk tradition in its own right.
D257.ctx: Composed in August 1815, one of dozens of songs Schubert wrote that extraordinarily productive year, setting a well-known Goethe poem already familiar to many of its first listeners.
facts: Composed during 1815, one of Schubert’s most prolific years for song.
Its melody has since passed into German folk tradition as a popular tune in its own right.
Sets a well-known poem by Goethe.

D531.about: A stark dialogue song in which Death gently but insistently persuades a terrified young woman to accompany him, its haunting piano introduction later reused by Schubert as the theme for the variation movement of his String Quartet ’Death and the Maiden’.
D531.ctx: Composed in February 1817, setting a poem by Matthias Claudius, and destined to become one of Schubert’s most enduring musical ideas after he returned to its opening theme seven years later in his D minor string quartet.
facts: Its opening theme was later reused as the basis for the slow movement of the String Quartet D. 810.
Sets a poem by Matthias Claudius structured as a dialogue between Death and a young woman.
Composed in 1817, several years before the quartet that borrows its theme.

D550.about: A bright, buoyant song about a trout darting in a stream, only for it to be caught by a cunning angler who muddies the water, a simple tale Schubert later used as the basis for the variation movement of his ’Trout’ Quintet.
D550.ctx: Composed around 1817, setting a poem by Christian Friedrich Daniel Schubart, and among the most immediately popular of Schubert’s songs even before its melody became still more famous through the piano quintet it inspired.
facts: Its melody forms the theme of the variation movement in the ’Trout’ Quintet, D. 667.
Sets a poem by Christian Friedrich Daniel Schubart.
One of the most widely recognized of all Schubert’s songs.

D547.about: A tender tribute to the art of music itself, thanking it for offering comfort in life’s darker hours, set to a simple, hymn-like melody that has made it one of Schubert’s most beloved and frequently performed songs.
D547.ctx: Composed around 1817, setting a poem by Schubert’s close friend Franz von Schober, a fellow member of his circle of writers, artists and musicians in Vienna.
facts: Sets a poem written by Schubert’s close friend Franz von Schober.
One of Schubert’s most consistently popular and frequently performed songs.
Its text is a direct address of gratitude to music itself.

D686.about: A gentle, hopeful song affirming faith that a new spring will always follow winter, its simple strophic form and warm melody making it one of Schubert’s most consoling settings.
D686.ctx: Composed in 1820, setting a poem by Ludwig Uhland, during a period when Schubert was increasingly active in Vienna’s literary and artistic circles alongside his growing reputation as a songwriter.
facts: Sets a poem by the German poet Ludwig Uhland.
Its title translates as ’Faith in Spring’.
Prized for its warm, consoling simplicity.

D774.about: A shimmering song evoking a boat gliding across rippling water at sunset, its constantly rippling piano accompaniment among Schubert’s most vivid pieces of musical word-painting.
D774.ctx: Composed in 1823, setting a poem attributed to Friedrich Leopold zu Stolberg-Stolberg, from a year in which Schubert also completed ’Die schöne Müllerin’ despite his declining health.
facts: Its rippling piano figuration vividly evokes water throughout.
Sets a poem long attributed to Friedrich Leopold zu Stolberg-Stolberg.
Composed the same year as the song cycle ’Die schöne Müllerin’.

D827.about: A hushed, deeply still song contrasting the sweetness of night and dreams with the return of harsh daylight, its slow-moving harmony and suspended sense of time making it one of Schubert’s most intensely inward songs.
D827.ctx: Composed either in 1822 or 1825 (sources differ), setting a poem by Matthäus von Collin, prized among singers and pianists alike for the exceptional stillness and control it demands.
facts: Sets a poem by Matthäus von Collin.
Noted for its unusually slow harmonic motion and suspended sense of time.
Widely regarded as one of the most difficult Schubert songs to sustain in performance.

D965.about: A late, unusually scored song for voice, clarinet and piano, written for a soprano who specifically requested something to show off both her voice and a virtuoso clarinetist together, ranging from pastoral serenity to exuberant, coloratura-filled joy.
D965.ctx: Composed in October 1828, weeks before Schubert’s death, at the request of the singer Anna Milder-Hauptmann, who wanted a piece combining voice and clarinet; Schubert reportedly had to be reminded more than once before completing it.
facts: Composed at the specific request of the soprano Anna Milder-Hauptmann.
One of the last works Schubert completed before his death.
Unusually scored for voice, clarinet and piano together.

D167.about: A compact, cheerful setting of the Latin Mass composed while Schubert was still a teenager, notably lighter in tone than the grander Masses he would write later in his short life.
D167.ctx: Composed in early 1815, likely intended for performance at the Lichtental parish church where Schubert had been baptized and where his First Mass had been premiered the previous year.
facts: Composed when Schubert was seventeen.
Likely intended for the Lichtental parish church associated with Schubert’s own baptism.
Not published until 1887, well over half a century after his death.

D950.about: The last and grandest of Schubert’s six Masses, composed in the final months of his life, notably omitting the words ’et unam sanctam catholicam ecclesiam’ from the Credo, a departure from convention that has prompted ongoing speculation about Schubert’s own religious views.
D950.ctx: Composed between June and September 1828, in the same final creative surge as the last three piano sonatas and the String Quintet, and never performed in Schubert’s lifetime.
facts: Composed in the last months of Schubert’s life, in the same period as his final piano sonatas.
Notably omits a clause from the traditional Latin text of the Creed.
Not performed publicly until after Schubert’s death.

D872.about: A setting of the Mass in German rather than Latin, written for community and congregational use, simpler and more direct than Schubert’s Latin Masses and intended to be singable by ordinary parishioners.
D872.ctx: Composed in 1826–27 on commission from a Viennese educator seeking a German-language Mass suitable for use in schools and parish congregations, reflecting a broader contemporary movement toward vernacular liturgical music.
facts: Sets the Mass text in German rather than the traditional Latin.
Composed for congregational and educational use rather than concert performance.
Simpler in style than Schubert’s six Latin Masses.
